title: Saturation products preserve kernels for a precise algebraic reason
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: Truncated addition gives an associative finite monoid whose minimal ideal is a single absorbing state. Taking products with these monoids preserves the cardinality of another monoid’s minimal ideal, while trajectory invariance follows separately from deterministic recursion.
definitions: For an integer k≥0 let L_k={0,…,k} with a⊕b=min(a+b,k). A two-sided ideal I of a monoid S is nonempty and satisfies SI∪IS⊂I.
For a finite monoid S, its kernel means its unique minimal nonempty two-sided ideal K(S). This meaning must be distinguished from the preimage of zero under a homomorphism.
A deterministic driven system has x_{t+1}=T(x_t,u_t), with a specified initial state.

result.name: Kernel of a product with saturating chains
result.statement: For any finite monoid S and finitely many k_i, K(S×∏L_{k_i})=K(S)×∏{k_i}. Hence its cardinality is |K(S)|. Two executions with the same initial state and identical input streams have identical trajectories.
result.proof: Associativity follows because both (a⊕b)⊕c and a⊕(b⊕c) equal min(a+b+c,k); zero is the identity and k is absorbing. Every nonempty ideal of L_k contains k, obtained by multiplying any of its elements by k, so {k} is minimal. In S×L_k, K(S)×{k} is an ideal. Conversely, from any (s,a) in an ideal, multiplication by (1,k) produces (s,k). Since the ideal SsS contains K(S), further left and right multiplications produce K(S)×{k}. Thus this is the minimal ideal. Iterate for finitely many coordinates. For trajectories, equality at time zero is assumed; equality at time t and equality of u_t give equality at t+1 by applying the same function T. Induction proves the assertion without any need for a compiler-specific theorem.

example.setup: Let S be the two-element group C₂ and adjoin L₂×L₃.
example.calculation: The product has 2·3·4=24 states, but its minimal ideal is C₂×{2}×{3}, containing exactly two states. Starting its saturating coordinates at (0,0) and adding (1,2) repeatedly gives (0,0),(1,2),(2,3),(2,3),…. The group coordinate can continue changing after saturation.

status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: Baby-step giant-step supplies a complete finite benchmark for the distinction between representation and inversion. Its correctness is elementary, whereas a low-dimensional encoding alone gives neither a short-vector promise nor an efficient way to identify the encoded answer.
definitions: Let G=⟨g⟩ be cyclic of known order n and h=g^x, with 0≤x<n. The task is to recover x.

status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: Future-trace equivalence gives a transition-compatible quotient and a minimal observable realization. A concrete parity machine shows why repeated state labels can be merged while finite traces only certify bounded-depth indistinguishability.
definitions: A deterministic observation machine consists of a finite state set S, alphabet Σ, transitions δ_a:S→S and output o:S→O.

result.statement: The relation ∼ is an equivalence compatible with every transition. Its quotient is observable, and any transition-respecting realization reproducing all outputs must distinguish its classes. For a finite machine, iterative output-partition refinement reaches ∼ after finitely many strict refinements.
result.proof: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity hold pointwise for each word. If s∼t, then for any word w the outputs after a followed by w agree, so δ_a s∼δ_a t. The kth partition equals ∼_k by induction. Any strict refinement increases the number of nonempty blocks, so there are at most |S|−1 strict refinements. title: Trace-estimator variance depends on the probe distribution
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: Independent Gaussian and Rademacher probes give equally unbiased trace estimates but different exact variances. Applying the calculation to a squared nonnormality commutator shows why a variance spike cannot be inferred without specifying the probe law.
definitions: Let B be a real symmetric n×n matrix and estimate tr B by T_m=m⁻¹∑_{r=1}^m z_rᵀBz_r, using independent probes with E[zzᵀ]=I.

For Gaussian entries Var(z_i²)=2, adding 2∑_iB_{ii}² gives 2tr B². For sign entries z_i²=1 exactly, so the entire diagonal part has zero variance. Averaging m independent samples divides each variance by m. The mean follows from E z_iz_j=δ_ij. This fourth-moment derivation also identifies what changes for complex probes or correlated sampling. Unbiasedness uses only second moments; variance requires the fourth moments and independence explicitly used above.
